catalog_quote: [p.47] The system that exists throughout LC is one of two basic tones, High (H ...) and Low (L ...), which may combine on a given syllable (with restricted and varying distribution) to give Falling (H+L ...), and less frequently, Rising (L+H ...) tones. ... In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !); i.e., the non-predictable lowering of H following another H, which has the effect of lowering the 'ceiling' for subsequent H tone realization. Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages. new_statements.rule_in_words: Etebi, like all Lower Cross languages in Connell's 19-language sample, is a two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone language with contrastive downstep; the author finds no real evidence for word-level stress in Lower Cross (explicitly rejecting Ward's 1933 verb-root stress for Efik and calling LC 'non-stress' languages), allowing only probable phrase-level stress and stress-like marking of compound junctures, which he says are uninvestigated.
new_statements.exceptions: Possible phrasal stress and stress at the juncture of compound elements (fn.32); Faraclas (1984b) analyses Obolo with phrasal stress and an extra-high tone; p.104 speculates word-position consonant weakening in Ibibio 'may be related to stress', unstudied.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level statement for Lower Cross as a whole (discussion framed around Efik/Ibibio, extended to 'the other LC languages'); Etebi is in the sample (own field data, wordlist citation forms) but has no dedicated prosody section. Word-level stress denied; phrase-level stress left open.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statements are group-level for Lower Cross (Connell's 19-language sample, which includes Etebi from his own fieldwork); the stress discussion is framed on Efik [efik1245]/Ibibio [ibib1240] and extended to 'the other LC languages'. No Etebi-specific prosodic description was found. Etebi (Esit Eket) is mutually intelligible with Ekit/Eket [ekit1245] (Connell 1991 p.10) and Wikipedia/Uyo authors group both as 'Ekid'; any future Ekid phonology would need checking for which variety it describes.

sources.note: Etebi is one of the 19 LC languages in the study (p.5, Table 2.1a p.41, p.42, appendix rows) but there is no Etebi-specific prosody section; all statements are group-level. p.47: throughout LC two basic tones H/L plus contrastive downstep, 'two-toned, terraced level languages'. pp.54-55: rejects Ward's (1933) verb-root stress for Efik, 'difficult to find any true evidence for stress'; fn.32 p.55: not asserting 'no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages' - likely phrasal stress and compound-juncture stress (cites Faraclas 1984b for Obolo); fn.34 p.56 calls LC 'a non-stress language';…
